Among 1,367 individuals infected with HIV who were tested, 383 (28%) were found to be seropositive for hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibodies. This data originates from the Hepatitis Testing Innovation Contest conducted in 2016, particularly in tuberculosis (TB) clinics. Populations such as people who inject drugs (PWID), prisoners, migrants, and individuals co-infected with HIV are key groups for targeted testing. The World Health Organization (WHO) already recommends routine HIV testing for all TB patients, including both active and presumptive cases, which has been shown to be highly acceptable. Integrating hepatitis B virus (HBV) and HCV testing into a comprehensive care package for TB patients is both feasible and acceptable, especially in settings and populations with high prevalence of TB and viral hepatitis. Sexually transmitted infection (STI) clinics are critical entry points for HIV and viral hepatitis prevention and treatment services, as HBV, HIV, and to a lesser extent HCV, are sexually transmissible infections. New diagnoses of STIs, such as gonorrhea and syphilis, can indicate recent unprotected sexual activity and help identify individuals at increased risk of acquiring HIV and viral hepatitis. WHO recommends routine HIV testing for individuals diagnosed with other STIs, with high uptake rates. Expanding this to include targeted HBV and HCV testing is likely to be both feasible and acceptable. Innovative care models have been developed to integrate hepatitis and opioid substitution therapy (OST) services for PWID within community drug treatment services, primarily in developed countries. These programs often include additional interventions such as education, harm reduction, mental health services, general medical care, and direct referrals for treatment. These models provide a framework for expanding viral hepatitis testing and treatment in low-income countries for at-risk populations. Hospital inpatient and outpatient settings offer opportunities for testing patients with symptoms or laboratory findings suggestive of viral hepatitis, such as unexplained abnormal liver function tests. Testing in hospitals, particularly in lowor concentrated-epidemic settings, has proven effective for HIV case-finding in Europe. Emergency departments have also been used to promote testing initiatives, such as the Going Viral campaign in London, which identified cases of HCV and HBV and linked many to care. Primary-care settings may be more accessible and less stigmatizing than hospital-based clinics, particularly for high-risk and vulnerable populations like PWID. Targeted case-finding for individuals with a history of injecting drug use can increase the number of people offered and accepting HCV testing. Integrated services, including drug and alcohol support and psychiatric care, are particularly effective for these populations, who often have multiple health comorbidities and complex needs. Peer-led or provider-led models with peer support can facilitate service integration in a way that is acceptable to high-risk groups. Electronic medical records (EMRs) can be used to flag high-risk primary care patients for testing. For example, in Philadelphia, community primary-care services integrated HCV testing and linkage to care, performing over 9,000 HCV tests between 2012 and 2016, with a significant proportion of positive cases linked to follow-up care and treatment. Pediatric and adolescent clinics are important settings for identifying undiagnosed HBV or HCV infections, particularly in high-prevalence countries. Testing children of parents with HBV or HCV infection, or those with symptoms or laboratory findings indicative of viral hepatitis, can identify many infections. This can be integrated into clinics already providing provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC) for HIV. Routine testing in antenatal clinics (ANC) is a key opportunity to reduce the global burden of HBV disease, primarily propagated through mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) in high-prevalence, resource-limited settings. Testing for HBsAg allows women to know their HBV serostatus and enables interventions to prevent MTCT, such as birth dose and infant HBV vaccination, hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG), and antiviral therapy. PITC for HBV in ANC has proven feasible and acceptable in several settings, though actual screening rates remain low in many high-burden lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Community-based testing can complement facility-based approaches, which may fail to reach certain high-risk populations, such as PWID, marginalized groups, or those in remote areas. Community-based testing has been shown to increase testing acceptance and uptake, achieve earlier diagnosis, and reach first-time testers and individuals who rarely use clinical services. However, barriers to linkage to care and treatment must be addressed. Mobile and outreach testing approaches include using mobile vans or tents at community sites, places of worship, entertainment venues, or public events. These services may be offered regularly, at night, or as one-time events linked to public gatherings. Door-to-door or home-based testing can also be effective, particularly when conducted during evenings or weekends to reach working individuals and men. Tailored HCV testing and linkage to care services for PWID are critical for delivering HCV services. Integration of HCV testing into PWID services, such as drug dependence treatment, needle and syringe programs, and community health services, has proven effective. For example, a methadone clinic in Kuala Lumpur screened and counseled individuals for HCV, collaborating with public hospitals to facilitate service integration after testing. Testing camps, such as those organized by the Community Network for Empowerment (CONE) in Manipur, India, provide free screening and confirmatory tests for HCV RNA, along with liver scans for staging liver fibrosis. These efforts have identified a significant number of HCV RNA-positive individuals, with linkage to treatment underway since the availability of direct-acting antivirals (DAAs). National testing campaigns aim to increase access to and uptake of testing, using facility-based, community-based, or combined approaches. However, challenges remain in ensuring linkage to care and treatment, as well as cost-effectiveness. Workplace testing provides access to employed individuals who may have limited access to clinical services but raises concerns about coercion, confidentiality breaches, and weak service linkages. Testing in schools, colleges, or other educational establishments can facilitate access to testing among sexually active young people, who may find it challenging to seek testing during school hours. These services can also provide sexual health education and counseling on risk reduction.
